intro: Marcelle Meyer plays the finale of Le Tombeau de Couperin: repeated notes start almost under the breath, then fill the keyboard. The Toccata carries its E-minor opening into an emphatic E-major finish.

sections.label: A · Repeated notes between the hands
sections.mNote: Quiet staccato semiquavers keep both hands busy

sections.label: B · A melody above the semiquavers
sections.mNote: Longer notes sing over the quick accompaniment

sections.label: Dev · Short figures cross the keyboard
sections.mNote: The hands exchange quick figures and sustained phrases

sections.label: Coda · Chords drive towards E major
sections.mNote: Repeated attacks grow into full chords and bass octaves

cues.title: Two hands on repeated notes
cues.text: Ravel begins pianissimo, with staccato semiquavers shared between the hands. The repeated notes have a dry, quick touch. Out of those tiny attacks he builds a finale that eventually needs almost the whole keyboard.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Toccata, p. 24: Vif, 2/4, pp, repeated semiquavers and staccato articulation. The final pages expand to chords and wide arpeggios.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Beethoven and Joseph de Marliave
cues.text: The Toccata remembers Captain Joseph de Marliave, a musicologist who writes about Beethoven’s string quartets and is killed in the First World War. His widow is the pianist Marguerite Long, who brings Ravel’s completed suite to the concert platform.
cues.evidence: BnF records the dedication and Long’s première: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. Marliave’s Beethoven scholarship: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_de_Marliave. His marriage and wartime death are documented at https://interlude.hk/the-dead-are-sad-enough-ravel-le-tombeau-de-couperin/.

cues.title: The widow at the piano
cues.text: Paris, 11 April 1919: Marguerite Long gives the first performance of the complete suite at the Salle Gaveau. Its last movement bears her husband’s name. The preceding movements carry the names of Ravel’s other friends lost in the war.
cues.evidence: BnF work authority gives the date, venue, pianist and all six dedications: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. The fourth movement commemorates two brothers, Pierre and Pascal Gaudin; the others each commemorate one man.

cues.title: A tune inside the hurry
cues.text: Long melodic notes stretch over the semiquavers. Ravel marks passages soutenu, sustained, so the singing notes hold their ground while the shorter ones keep moving. The pianist has to give both kinds of touch at once.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Toccata, middle pages; Piano Practical Editions, bars 130–170, including p soutenu at bar 166. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP560971-PMLP4975-Le_Tombeau_de_Couperin.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Four sharps at the finish
cues.text: The final page opens out into E major, with four sharps and a fortississimo flourish. The repeated notes have become full chords, reinforced by low octaves. Ravel ends the suite with a sharp, ringing stop.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Toccata, p. 32; Piano Practical Editions, bars 240–247, p. 52: E-major signature, fff and final E-major chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Long notes over quick ones
transitions.from: A · Repeated notes between the hands
transitions.to: B · A melody above the semiquavers
transitions.how: The piano keeps its semiquavers while a longer melodic line emerges above them. Sustained notes and slurs ask for a singing right hand; the accompanying notes still need the opening’s light touch. Ravel holds the quick two-beat bar through the change.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Toccata, pp. 27–29: sustained melody above active accompaniment in 2/4. The existing section boundary places the passage.

transitions.title: The bass joins the charge
transitions.from: Dev · Short figures cross the keyboard
transitions.to: Coda · Chords drive towards E major
transitions.how: The piano’s repeated attacks expand into chords, with a stronger bass beneath them. The crescendo carries this last stretch towards the four-sharp E-major ending. Even at the broadest chordal statements, semiquavers continue to propel the hands.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Toccata, pp. 30–32; Piano Practical Editions, closing pages, culminating in E major at bar 240.

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
